clue.text: Not much on the bird table? Stone the crows!

definitions.text: Not much on the bird table?

blocks.clueFragment: Not much on the bird table?
blocks.note: first meaning: the small scraps of bread left out for birds
second meaning: a mild exclamation of surprise

explanation.walkthrough: The birds in both halves make it look like one garden scene; 'Stone the crows!' is a British exclamation of astonishment, as is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Scraps of bread scattered for birds are a meagre offering, and the same word is a dated British interjection of surprise.

clue.text: Sailing boats, cutters

blocks.note: first meaning: fast nineteenth-century merchant ships
second meaning: a tool for trimming hair or nails

explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is also a kind of sailing boat, so the clue looks like a list of vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: Clippers were fast sailing ships, and the same word names shears or nail trimmers.

clue.text: Employment centre in busy period

indicators.note: centre in points at the middle letters of the word that follows

blocks.note: the two middle letters
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A job centre is at its most frantic during the rush.
explanation.walkthrough: Employment centre reads as a jobcentre, but employment alone is the definition and centre is the selecting signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means the use or employment of something, as in the employment of a word.

clue.text: Very hot grease in house, finally wiped

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is wiped away
in means placed inside the other piece

blocks.note: house, or housey-housey, is an old British name for bingo, the numbers game
oil is a lubricant

explanation.surface: Scalding fat at home, eventually cleaned off.
explanation.walkthrough: In the British game of bingo a winner calls House!, so house can stand for the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Boiling is used informally to describe weather or a room that is extremely warm.

clue.text: Second small animal in capital city

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a very short time
S is the standard abbreviation for small
a cow is a farm animal

explanation.surface: A second small creature has turned up somewhere in a capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow is the capital of Russia, so it is an example of a capital city.

clue.text: Circling piece, test circles!

indicators.note: circles means goes around, so the test surrounds the piece

blocks.note: a bit is a piece
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: An examination question about something that goes round and round.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbital path is one that goes around a body, so the adjective means revolving around.

clue.text: Old man Morgan wrong to gatecrash party

indicators.note: a name gone wrong has its letters disordered
a gatecrasher gets inside the event uninvited

blocks.note: taken as written
Con is short for the Conservative Party

explanation.surface: An elderly Mr Morgan is in the wrong for barging into a party uninvited.
explanation.walkthrough: Old man looks like it describes Morgan, but it is the definition: early humans.
explanation.definitionFit: Cro-Magnon was an early modern human of the Stone Age, a man of very ancient times.

clue.text: Confused — like sheep?

blocks.note: first meaning: vague or muddled in thought
second meaning: covered in fleece

explanation.walkthrough: Sheep are proverbially muddled followers, so the two senses look like one.
explanation.definitionFit: Muddled thinking is called woolly, and the literal sense is made of or covered in fleece.

clue.text: Mixture of it with a rum is sweet

indicators.note: a mixture stirs its ingredients together, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook observes that stirring rum into something makes a lovely pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the real dessert is soaked in alcohol, so the recipe-like surface nearly describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiramisu is an Italian layered dessert, and a sweet is the British word for a dessert course.

clue.text: Appalling — like an impossible tongue-twister?

blocks.note: first meaning: too dreadful to be described
second meaning, read literally: unable to be said aloud

explanation.walkthrough: The second half takes the figurative word literally: a tongue-twister no one can pronounce.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unspeakable is too horrible to mention, and literally a phrase that cannot be uttered.

clue.text: Couple of shockers, one's a mistake

blocks.note: boo is said to give someone a fright, and a couple means it appears twice

explanation.surface: Of two dreadful performances, one turns out to be an error.
explanation.walkthrough: Shockers suggests terrible displays, but here it means things that startle: the word shouted to make someone jump.
explanation.definitionFit: A booboo is an informal word for a silly blunder or slip.

clue.text: Weapon confiscated by the peerage

indicators.note: something confiscated is held inside another's keeping, so the answer sits within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A lord's sword has been seized by the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: An epee is a fencing sword, so it is a kind of weapon.

clue.text: Voracious broadcasting of banalities

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters things widely, so the letters that follow are spread into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that the airwaves are greedily stuffed with trite programmes.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe an appetite that can never be satisfied, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Washington writer, capital US composer!

blocks.note: Washington Irving was the American author of Rip Van Winkle
Berlin is the capital of Germany

explanation.surface: An American author from the capital, Washington, is hailed as a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Washington looks like the US capital, but it is the first name of the writer; the capital is a different city altogether.
explanation.definitionFit: Irving Berlin wrote American songs such as White Christmas, making him a celebrated US songwriter.

clue.text: Present reduction all over the shop

indicators.note: a British idiom for scattered in disarray, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopper notes that today's price cut applies throughout the store.
explanation.walkthrough: Present looks like a noun or the current moment, but it is a verb: to present one person to another.
explanation.definitionFit: To present someone is to make them known to another person, the same as the verb.

clue.text: Officially consider row more jovial

blocks.note: a court hears a case, examining it formally
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: Formally weighing up a quarrel makes everyone more cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: Row suggests a quarrel, but here it means a line of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartier is the comparative of hearty, meaning warmly cheerful and exuberant.

clue.text: Tough — as a jumbo, perhaps?

blocks.note: first meaning: unaffected by criticism or insults
second meaning, read literally: an elephant has a hide of great thickness

explanation.walkthrough: Jumbo is a nickname for an elephant, whose hide really is thick, so the figurative phrase is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hard to wound with criticism is resilient, and an elephant's hide is literally heavy and dense.

clue.text: Nationality in Ireland (and having gone abroad), as I organised

indicators.note: something gone abroad has left, so those letters leave the country's name
organised means arranged anew, so the remaining letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
these letters are the ones removed
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sorts out a nationality for a person who has emigrated from Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the three letters of 'and' from the island's name to leave IREL, then shuffle in AS and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Israeli names the citizenship of someone from Israel, so it is an example of a nationality.

clue.text: Coverage of joint record in work at bakery

indicators.note: in means placed inside the other piece

blocks.note: an EP is an extended-play record
bakers work dough by kneading it

explanation.surface: A press report on a joint record deal for working in a bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: Joint suggests a cut of meat at a bakery or a shared record, but it is the knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A kneepad is protective padding worn over the knee, which is a joint of the leg.

clue.text: Grave pub altercation

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
a row is a noisy quarrel

explanation.surface: A serious fight breaks out in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Grave reads as an adjective meaning serious, but it is the noun: a burial place.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrow is an ancient burial mound, a prehistoric tomb heaped with earth.

clue.text: Good story about a very old urn, abridged

indicators.note: an abridged text is cut short, so the last letter of the preceding word goes
about means surrounding, so the tale wraps around the words that follow

blocks.note: a fable is a short moral tale
taken as written
V is the standard abbreviation for very
O is the abbreviation for old
taken as written before it is shortened

explanation.surface: A shortened account of an ancient urn is pleasingly told.
explanation.walkthrough: The story opens after its first letter to take in the other pieces: F, then A, V, O and the clipped urn, then ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A favourable report or result is a good one, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Unnecessarily criticise swimmer

blocks.note: first meaning: to complain or find fault pettily
second meaning: a freshwater fish

explanation.walkthrough: Swimmer suggests a person in a pool, but crosswords often use it for a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To nag with petty complaints is one sense of the verb, and the noun is a common freshwater fish.

clue.text: Boat trade

blocks.note: first meaning: a vessel
second meaning: a skilled occupation

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests boatbuilding or shipping, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel on water is a craft, and a skilled manual occupation is also a craft.

clue.text: Band in detailed rug containing first of roses

indicators.note: read as de-tailed, the word loses its tail, its final letter
first of asks for only the opening letter of the next word
containing means holding inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a rug is slang for a hairpiece
the initial letter of the flowers

explanation.surface: A band is woven into an intricate rug with a rose motif.
explanation.walkthrough: Detailed looks like an adjective for an ornate rug; split it as de-tailed. A rug is slang for a wig.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a group of performers, so it is a band in the sense of a company of players.

clue.text: Stress in rigging of same ship

indicators.note: rigging means fixing or manipulating, so the following letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Strain on the ropes and masts of the very vessel we sailed on.
explanation.walkthrough: Rigging fits the nautical picture as the ropes of a ship, but here it means fixing or tampering with.
explanation.definitionFit: Stress and emphasis both mean the importance or weight placed on a word or idea.

clue.text: Not much to eat? This is sad to see

blocks.note: first meaning, whimsically: a small pastry, a tiny bit of food
second meaning: a sentimental film that makes viewers cry

explanation.walkthrough: The first half splits the answer as wee plus pie, wee being Scottish for small; the second is a tear-jerking film.
explanation.definitionFit: A weepie is an informal term for a tearful melodrama in film, written to make audiences cry.

clue.text: Journalist taking part in foxtrot I deliberately knocked over

indicators.note: taking part in means being a part of, so the answer lies within the following words
something knocked over is upended, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the dance, the I and the start of the adverb

explanation.surface: A newspaper writer dancing a foxtrot confesses to deliberately bumping into someone.
explanation.definitionFit: An editor is a senior journalist who prepares and oversees what a paper publishes.
